CleanAir guide

Understand your air quality readings

What PM2.5, TVOC and CO₂ can tell you, and why the readings describe different conditions.

PM2.5 describes fine particles

PM2.5 refers to airborne particles with a diameter of 2.5 micrometres or smaller. Particle levels can vary with activities and conditions, so look at patterns rather than a single reading.

TVOC combines multiple compounds

Total volatile organic compounds is a combined measurement. It does not identify every individual substance or its risk. Changes may help you investigate activities, products or ventilation in a room.

CO₂ is a different kind of signal

Carbon dioxide can rise in occupied rooms with limited fresh air exchange. It is a useful part of a ventilation discussion. A purification device does not replace fresh air exchange, and CO₂ alone does not describe every air quality concern.

Temperature and humidity add context

These readings describe environmental conditions. Consider them alongside activities, occupancy and the sensor’s placement when reviewing room trends.

Use live readings and historical trends together

A connected dashboard helps you compare the current reading with earlier conditions. Note occupancy, operating hours and activities when reviewing changes. Discuss reporting, alerts and any BMS integration requirements with the team.

Read the pattern, then ask the right question

Compare readings over time and note what was happening in the space. A monitor provides information; it does not identify every pollutant or replace an appropriate assessment. Ask the team about sensor configuration, placement and data access.
